title: The Maritime Lord Who Made a Kingdom
bullets: Unified Silla rotted from within under the rigid bone-rank system, and by around 900 the peninsula cracked into the Later Three Kingdoms: Gyeon Hwon's Later Baekje and Gung Ye's Taebong.
Wang Geon, a merchant-lord from the trading port of Songak, was offered the throne when Gung Ye's generals mutinied in 918; he named his kingdom Goryeo, a deliberate claim on ancient Goguryeo.
The name traveled with Arab and Persian merchants and a chain of European mapmakers, becoming Corea then Korea: the world's name for the peninsula is the brand of this one dynasty.
Wang Geon moved the capital to his home port, renamed Gaegyeong (modern Kaesong), and rebuilt Pyongyang as a Western Capital to anchor a lifelong policy of northern expansion.
After near-disaster at the Battle of Gongsan in 927, Goryeo reunified the peninsula by 936: Silla's last king surrendered peacefully in 935 and Later Baekje was crushed at Iljiwon.

To bind the warlords, Wang Geon married 29 wives from rival clans and granted revocable merit land, converting armed magnates into an aristocracy whose money and grandchildren depended on the dynasty.
His deathbed Ten Injunctions of 943 read like a constitution, but the marriage web detonated at once: the magnate Wanggyu's 945 rebellion was the first sign of a throne floating on armed in-laws.

title: Building a State Out of Warlords
bullets: Goryeo began as a confederation with a crown on top; two kings turned it into a real bureaucratic state, the least dramatic and most important transformation in the dynasty's history.
Gwangjong's Slave Review Act of 956 freed the war-enslaved, draining the magnates' private armies and refilling the crown's tax rolls in a single stroke.
On Ssang Gi's advice, Gwangjong instituted the gwageo civil service examination in 958: office by tested merit, a system Western Europe would not match for nearly a thousand years.
Behind the reforms ran terror: through the 960s Gwangjong purged the founding merit aristocracy with mass treason charges, leaving the throne supreme but the elite traumatized.
The Jeonsigwa land system tied land revenue to bureaucratic rank, and its slow capture by hereditary families is one of the deep clocks ticking under the entire dynasty.
Choe Seungno's 28-point memorial of 982 became the blueprint for Seongjong's Confucian state: chancelleries, Six Ministries, twelve provincial mok, and the Gukjagam academy.
Korea's first coinage failed because the economy was too local to need coins, while Song China was already running a cash economy and issued the world's first paper money in 1024.
By Seongjong's death Goryeo was one of the world's more sophisticated states, just as the regicide of 1009 by the general Gangjo handed the Khitan a pretext for invasion.

title: The Khitan Storm
bullets: The Khitan were Mongolic-speaking steppe nomads whose Liao empire, founded by Abaoji in 916, dominated northern China and forced even Song China into humiliating tribute.
In the first invasion of 993 the envoy Seo Hui out-argued the Khitan general face to face, conceding nominal submission while winning Goryeo the territory up to the Yalu River.
The second invasion of 1010 saw the Liao emperor sack Gaegyeong and burn the palace; King Hyeonjong fled the length of the country to Naju before a negotiated withdrawal.
Out of that terror King Hyeonjong vowed the first Tripitaka Koreana in 1011, carving the entire Buddhist canon onto thousands of woodblocks as a state act of faith.
In the third invasion the scholar-general Gang Gam-chan let the Khitan overextend, then annihilated them at Gwiju in 1019; barely a few thousand of 100,000 escaped and Liao never invaded again.
The tactic echoed Eulji Mundeok's destruction of a Sui army at the Salsu River in 612, a recurring Korean answer to being outnumbered.
Victory bought a century: Goryeo built the Cheolli Jangseong border wall, balanced Liao and Song by triangular diplomacy, and traded with Arab and Persian Daesik merchants.

title: Celadon and Its Cracks
bullets: Goryeo perfected sanggam inlaid celadon, ranked first under heaven by Song connoisseurs, alongside hanji paper exported as the world's finest and dense astronomical records still used today.
The monk-prince Uicheon tried to heal Buddhism's split between the scripture-focused Gyo schools and the meditation-focused Seon school, founding a Korean Cheontae school in 1097 as a compromise.
Beneath the brilliance the aristocracy steadily captured the Jeonsigwa land system, hardening into a hereditary caste sitting on top of the bureaucratic machinery rather than inside it.
Foreign humiliation stung: Yun Gwan's Nine Forts against the Jurchen were abandoned by 1109, and after the Jurchen founded the Jin empire Goryeo submitted to it by 1126.
Yi Ja-gyeom's 1126 coup, an in-law magnate seizing the throne and burning the palace, proved the dynasty's center could be captured by a single overgrown family.
Myocheong's 1135 revolt to move the capital to Pyongyang and declare an empire was a war over Goryeo's very identity, crushed by the Confucian statesman Kim Bu-sik.
In 1145 Kim Bu-sik presented the Samguk Sagi, the oldest surviving Korean history, invaluable and pointedly Silla-centered because his own family ran back to the Silla royal house.
Under King Uijong the civil aristocracy's century of contempt for the despised military officer class became theatrical, drying out the powder for the explosion of 1170.

title: The Generals Take Over
bullets: In 1170 humiliated officers led by Jeong Jung-bu massacred the civil officials, deposed King Uijong, and ended two centuries of civilian aristocratic government in an afternoon of blood.
The strongman Gyeong Dae-seung built the Dobang, a private household army; whoever commanded the best household troops was the government, no matter who sat on the throne.
Yi Ui-min, son of a peddler and a temple slave, clawed to the top of the state purely through the army: a savage social revolution the people at the bottom noticed.
Choe Chungheon seized power in 1196 and, alone among the strongmen, kept it, founding a sixty-year hereditary dictatorship by ruling through the Gyojeong Dogam instead of taking the crown.
The slave Manjeok organized a 1198 uprising asking whether generals and ministers were a matter of birth; the plot was betrayed and the regime's answer was the river.
Goryeo's first contact with the Mongols came in 1219 against Khitan remnants, and it came with a bill: crushing tribute demands and overbearing envoys.
When a Mongol envoy was killed on the border in 1225 the Mongols broke relations and, six years later, returned to collect with the largest army Korea had ever seen.

title: The Mongol Cataclysm
bullets: The Mongols had built the largest contiguous land empire in history; against it Goryeo had a sixty-year military dictatorship and a wall built to stop Khitan cavalry.
In 1232 the dictator Choe U moved the court to Ganghwa Island, safe behind extreme tides, while the mainland population was left to absorb the Mongol army essentially undefended.
The fighting was done by the commoners, monks, and slaves the island court had abandoned; one campaign of 1254 alone carried off over 200,000 Koreans as captives.
The Mongols burned the original Tripitaka Koreana and the 250-foot Hwangnyongsa pagoda, the tallest wooden building in East Asia, never rebuilt.
On the safe island Goryeo re-carved the canon onto 81,258 woodblocks, the most accurate Buddhist canon in existence, still intact today at Haeinsa.
The same besieged island produced the first cast-metal movable type around 1234, two centuries before Gutenberg, and the first Korean medical text, the Hyangyak Gugeupbang.
After the Choe dictatorship fell in 1258, the crown prince bet on Kublai in the Mongol succession war; Kublai won and let Goryeo survive as a kingdom rather than an erased province.
The court returned to the mainland in 1270, ending a century of military rule, but the Sambyeolcho fought on as a rebellion until annihilated in 1273.

title: The Son-in-Law Nation
bullets: Goryeo alone among the major settled states the Mongols fought kept its own royal house, because one prince had bet early on Kublai and Kublai remembered.
From 1274 Goryeo kings were Mongol imperial sons-in-law, raised at Dadu, wearing the Mongol queue, and stamped with the loyal-to-the-Yuan prefix Chung.
Goryeo was forced to build the fleets for the invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281, both wrecked by the typhoons the Japanese called the kamikaze.
The Mongols amputated territory directly, including the Ssangseong Commandery and Jeju Island as a horse pasture whose stamp outlasted the dynasty.
The Yuan demanded tribute women; one Goryeo-born palace woman became Empress Gi, effectively running the inner Yuan court by the 1340s.
Under domination the monk Iryeon compiled the Samguk Yusa around 1281, preserving the Dangun foundation legend as a quiet act of defiance disguised as a story collection.
The century's transformative import was Neo-Confucianism: a total theory of reality, received in its Yuan-canonized exam form, that gave scholars standing to call the existing order cosmically wrong.
An Hyang revived the academy and the sadaebu scholar class formed; King Chungseon's 1298 reform failed, proving the new idea could not yet win from inside the system.

title: Reform, Collapse, and the Birth of Joseon
bullets: King Gongmin, raised at the dying Yuan court, purged the pro-Yuan Gi clan in 1356, abolished the Mongol oversight organs, and recovered the Ssangseong Commandery in a single bold year.
Recovering the northeast brought in the frontier family of Yi Ja-chun and his son Yi Seong-gye, the family that would end the dynasty.
Red Turban rebels sacked Gaegyeong in 1361 while Japanese wokou pirates raided the coast, hammering a dynasty trying to reinvent itself from both land and sea.
Gongmin handed reform to the low-born monk Sin Don, whose land and slave directorate was wildly popular below and a declaration of war above; the aristocracy won in the king's ear.
Sin Don was executed in 1371 and Gongmin assassinated in 1374: top-down reform had failed again, fatally, killing the last chance of saving Goryeo as Goryeo.
Choe Mu-seon's Firearms Directorate built Korea's first cannon, destroying a wokou fleet at Jinpo in 1380; the Jikji was printed with movable metal type in 1377, 78 years before Gutenberg.
Ordered to invade Ming Liaodong, Yi Seong-gye turned his army around at Wihwa Island in 1388, seized the government, and sent Choe Yeong to his death.
The Gwajeon Law of 1391 burned the old land registers and destroyed the aristocracy's economic base; in 1392 Jeong Mong-ju was killed on the Seonjuk Bridge and Yi Seong-gye founded Joseon.
